papers.selection_reason: Introduces a collective learning paradigm (CEL) and a specific fine-tuning method (FERT) for robot fleets, directly addressing robot manipulation and learning from deployment experience.
papers.title: Learning from Fleet Experience: A Collective Learning Paradigm for Robots
papers.tldr: Collective experience learning lets robot fleets improve a shared policy from deployment failures and successful trajectories without additional expert corrections, achieving high reliability across manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Data-driven learning for general-purpose robotic manipulation presents a fundamental trade-off between data-collection cost and adaptability to real-world environments. Imitation learning (IL) requires costly human demonstrations, whereas simulation-based learning is vulnerable to sim-to-real gaps in dynamics and sensor observations. We propose ReDOA (Real-World Distillation via Observation Alignment), a framework that decouples control learning from perception learning to learn image-based policies in the real world. A state-based teacher policy trained in simulation is executed on a real robot, and its control knowledge is distilled into an image-based student policy using the collected trajectories. Observation Alignment resolves observation mismatches between data collection and deployment. This framework collects successful, efficiently executed trajectories paired with real-world visual observations, without requiring demonstrations from human experts. In real-robot experiments on three non-prehensile manipulation tasks, including bimanual manipulation, our method achieves better overall performance when jointly considering task success and execution efficiency than both IL based on human demonstrations and policy distillation in simulation. https://isri-aist.github.io/redoa-project-page/
authors: Kotaro Kajitsuka
Masaki Murooka
Fumio Kanehiro
bullets: Addresses the cost of human demonstrations and the sim-to-real gap in dynamics and visual observations.
Uses a state-based teacher trained in simulation to guide an image-based student through real-robot trajectories.
Observation Alignment bridges mismatches between observations during data collection and deployment.
Evaluated on three real-robot non-prehensile manipulation tasks, including bimanual manipulation.
Reports better combined task success and execution efficiency than human-demonstration IL and simulation-based distillation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes ReDOA, a real-world distillation framework for image-based manipulation policies that decouples control from perception, addressing sim-to-real gaps in robotic manipulation.
papers.title: ReDOA: Real-World Distillation via Observation Alignment for Image-Based Manipulation Policy Learning
papers.tldr: ReDOA distills a simulation-trained state policy into a real-world image-based policy by aligning observations, avoiding human demonstrations while improving manipulation success and efficiency.

papers.abstract: It has long been proposed that animals construct cognitive maps to support flexible behavior in novel environments. We tested whether large language models form similar representations using relational reasoning tasks and causal "mosaic experiments" that manipulate internal activations in open-weight language models. Models beyond the ten-billion-parameter scale successfully inferred unstated relationships between entities and generalized to synthetic entity names. Across model and task families, models generated abstract representations of relational structure and combined them additively with representations of entity identity, binding entities to roles within that structure. Models stored observed relationships as pairwise links that they composed retrospectively when queried, rather than prospectively positioning each entity in a global coordinate system. Binding was mediated by a sparse, distributed set of key--value pairs; by perturbing these pairs, we implanted "false memories" that altered model behavior in predictable ways. Overall, our findings reveal an internal organization analogous to a cognitive map that explains how language models reason with limited information.
authors: Albert Qin, Jonathan Cohen, Gautam Reddy
bullets: Models larger than 10 billion parameters inferred unstated relationships and generalized them to synthetic entity names.
Causal activation experiments found abstract relational structure combined additively with entity-identity representations.
Models represented relationships as pairwise links composed at query time, rather than as positions in a global coordinate system.
Entity–role binding relied on sparse, distributed key–value representations; perturbing them produced predictable false memories.
These findings suggest an internal organization analogous to a cognitive map for reasoning with limited information.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates internal relational representations and key-value binding in large language models, contributing to LLM understanding and interpretability.
papers.title: Cognitive Map in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Large language models can build cognitive-map-like relational representations that support flexible inference and targeted memory manipulation.

papers.abstract: Large-scale action pretraining equips Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs) with strong manipulation capabilities, with particular strengths in generalization and closed-loop robustness, but reproducing such pretraining requires substantial robot data and computation. To transfer these capabilities from pretrained EFMs to policies without action pretraining, we introduce TILDE (Teacher-In-the-Loop Distillation from EFMs), which synergizes on-policy distillation at student-induced states with learning from teacher-executed recovery trajectories. We further propose AutoDAgger, an autonomous data aggregation pipeline in which a robotic reward model is utilized to monitor task progress and trigger teacher intervention, thereby collecting recovery experience without human monitoring or manual control. AutoDAgger accelerates recovery-trajectory collection by more than $2\times$ compared with the human-in-the-loop method. By unifying learning from demonstrations, on-policy teacher supervision, and teacher's corrective behavior, TILDE improves task performance by up to $4.1\times$ over behavior cloning across three real-world tasks and supports effective cross-architecture distillation.
authors: Yuxiang Lu, Yantong Liu, Jinghua Hou, Xueli Sun, Ruihua Han, Zhe Liu, Hengshuang Zhao
bullets: Targets the high data and compute costs of reproducing EFM action pretraining.
Combines learning from demonstrations, on-policy teacher supervision, and teacher-executed recovery trajectories.
Introduces AutoDAgger, which uses a robotic reward model to detect progress and autonomously trigger teacher intervention.
Collects recovery trajectories over 2× faster than a human-in-the-loop approach.
Improves task performance by up to 4.1× over behavior cloning across three real-world tasks and enables cross-architecture distillation.
papers.selection_reason: Distills embodied foundation model manipulation skills into student policies using on-policy teacher supervision and autonomous recovery-trajectory collection.
papers.title: TILDE: Teacher-in-the-Loop Distillation from Embodied Foundation Models
papers.tldr: TILDE distills robust manipulation skills from pretrained Embodied Foundation Models into policies without requiring action pretraining or human-supervised recovery collection.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly judged by how well they rank plausible futures, yet plausibility alone is the wrong target. The same scene can evolve under many latent rules, and a future that is smooth and physically valid under one rule can be incoherent under the rule actually in force. We formalize the resulting failure, operator-blindness, and show that it is systematically hidden by standard evaluation: a scorer can attain near-perfect generic ranking while separating current-world from other-world futures no better than chance. We introduce Operator-Mismatch Contrastive (OMC) learning, whose semantic hard negatives are valid-but-wrong-operator trajectories, and a matching protocol that measures world-relative coherence directly. On a controlled synthetic benchmark with in- and out-of-distribution operator parameters, across two trajectory-scoring backbones, and on feature-level external validation with CoPhy ballsCF, OMC raises operator-sensitive scoring far above a chance baseline that nonetheless achieves 0.99 generic top-1. We prove that the wrong-operator negative is necessary both for the protocol to detect the failure and for the objective to fix it, and position OMC as an auxiliary coherence signal (a trajectory-coherence scorer, not a generative model, planner, or control agent) that can be attached to existing world-model representations.
authors: One Octadion, Firmansyah Sundana, Novanto Yudistira
bullets: Standard plausibility ranking can miss operator-blindness: generic ranking may be near-perfect while world-relative discrimination remains at chance.
OMC uses valid-but-wrong-operator trajectories as semantic hard negatives.
A matching protocol directly measures coherence with the operator governing the current world.
Across synthetic in- and out-of-distribution settings, two scoring backbones, and CoPhy ballsCF validation, OMC substantially improves operator-sensitive scoring.
The analysis proves wrong-operator negatives are necessary both to expose and correct the failure; OMC is an auxiliary scorer, not a generator, planner, or controller.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces operator-sensitive trajectory coherence scoring with wrong-operator hard negatives, directly targeting world-model evaluation and representations.
papers.title: Operator-Mismatch Contrastive Learning for World-Relative Trajectory Coherence
papers.tldr: OMC learning trains world-model scorers to distinguish futures that are valid under the current world dynamics from those valid under a different operator.

papers.abstract: Hybrid architectures offer a promising approach to efficient language modeling by combining a small number of full-attention layers with a larger number of efficient sequence layers, such as sparse attention and recurrent layers. While full-attention layers maintain a KV cache that grows linearly with sequence length, efficient layers typically rely on separate, fixed-size states rather than accessing this richer existing memory. Recent work has begun exploring ways to allow efficient layers access to the KV cache, but the theoretical benefits of such access, and the extent to which existing approaches can realize them remain poorly understood. We investigate these questions by analyzing the expressive power of individual hybrid blocks on function composition, a well-studied task in sequence-model expressivity associated with multi-hop reasoning. We first establish that both conventional hybrid blocks and those with top-$\kappa$ KV-cache access require $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ capacity to compute even two-function composition over a domain of size $n$. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the \emph{Multi-hop Retrieval Attention} (MuRA) hybrid block, a simple architecture that enables multi-hop retrieval from a shared KV cache while preserving asymptotic computational and memory efficiency. We prove that a single fixed size $m$-hop MuRA block can compute $m$-function composition, whereas computing $(m+1)$-function composition with the same retrieval depth requires polynomial model size, establishing a strict expressivity hierarchy in retrieval depth. Synthetic experiments support this hierarchy, showing that increasing retrieval depth enables learning progressively deeper compositions, substantially outperforming existing hybrid architectures. Together, our results identify multi-hop retrieval as a promising mechanism for improving the expressive power of efficient hybrid architectures.
authors: Yam Eitan, Gilad Yehudai, Haggai Maron
bullets: Hybrid models combine a few full-attention layers with more efficient sparse-attention or recurrent layers, but efficient layers typically cannot exploit the full KV cache.
Conventional hybrid blocks and top-κ KV-cache access require Ω(√n) capacity even for two-function composition over a domain of size n.
The proposed Multi-hop Retrieval Attention (MuRA) block supports multi-hop access to a shared KV cache while preserving asymptotic computational and memory efficiency.
A fixed-size m-hop MuRA block can compute m-function composition, while computing (m+1)-function composition at the same depth requires polynomial model size.
Synthetic experiments support a retrieval-depth hierarchy, with deeper retrieval enabling progressively deeper compositions and outperforming existing hybrid architectures.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a multi-hop retrieval attention block for efficient hybrid language architectures, improving expressivity while preserving asymptotic efficiency.
papers.title: Improving the Expressive Power of Hybrid Sequence Models via Multi-Hop Retrieval
papers.tldr: Multi-hop retrieval substantially increases the expressive power of efficient hybrid sequence models, enabling deeper compositional reasoning with fixed-size retrieval depth.

papers.abstract: Federated learning for capacity-heterogeneous clients and federated continual learning are each well studied on their own, but their intersection -- clients holding differently sized models while every client's data stream also drifts over time -- remains underexplored. We study this setting directly, training a ResNet-18 fleet from scratch on Split-CIFAR-100 (10 tasks, class-incremental), and introduce DROD (Dual-Ratio Ordered Dropout), which builds on FjORD's Ordered Dropout by using two independent reduction axes to extract sub-models: a shortcut ratio and a branch ratio. On a shared parameter/FLOP budget ladder, DROD achieves the highest mean accuracy among the heterogeneous-model federated learning strategies we compare. Its advantage over the two strongest baseline geometries persists across every replay-buffer size we test and under ER, DER++, and BiC; under EWC, all three geometries collapse alike.
authors: Berk Sezer, \"Ozg\"ur Soysal
bullets: Addresses the underexplored combination of device capacity heterogeneity and drifting client data.
Extends FjORD’s Ordered Dropout with two independent sub-model reduction axes: shortcut ratio and branch ratio.
Evaluated with ResNet-18 models trained from scratch on Split-CIFAR-100 across 10 class-incremental tasks.
Outperforms the two strongest baseline geometries across tested replay-buffer sizes under ER, DER++, and BiC.
Under EWC, DROD and the comparison geometries perform similarly, indicating a scope limitation.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses continual learning of models on drifting data streams under federated heterogeneous-device settings.
papers.title: DROD: Dual-Ratio Ordered Dropout for Federated Continual Learning on Heterogeneous Devices
papers.tldr: DROD enables federated continual learning with differently sized client models and achieves the best mean accuracy among compared heterogeneous-model strategies in the studied setting.

papers.abstract: We empirically analyze two recently proposed encoder-free multimodal LLMs, Gemma-4 12B and Inkling-Small. Unlike previous multimodal LLMs, these models do not use modality-specific encoders to extract tokenized embeddings representing audio and image input; instead, they directly feed windows of samples, pixels, or spectral features to the Transformer language model. We analyze whether the early layers of these models learn to function similarly to dedicated audio and visual encoders. We find that these early layers do in fact act as ``implicit encoders,'' encoding audio and visual inputs in a way that is largely invariant to their cross-modal context. Furthermore, when performing multimodal reasoning tasks, we show that independently encoding the modalities throughout these early model layers achieves the same accuracy as jointly encoding them from the first layer onwards. Finally, we use layer-wise probing to analyze the salient information captured by the implicit encoders and find their behavior to be similar to several popular encoder models.
authors: David Harwath, Desh Raj, Xavier Velez, Sandra Arcos-Holzinger, Willie Jeng, Karen Livescu, Leibny Paola Garcia-Perera, Sanjeev Khudanpur
bullets: Analyzes Gemma-4 12B and Inkling-Small, which process raw audio and image features without dedicated modality-specific encoders.
Finds that early layers encode audio and visual inputs in ways that are largely invariant to cross-modal context.
Shows that independently encoding modalities through early layers matches the accuracy of jointly encoding them from the first layer.
Layer-wise probing indicates that the learned representations capture salient information similarly to several established encoder models.
papers.selection_reason: Empirically analyzes implicit encoders in encoder-free multimodal LLMs (Gemma-4, Inkling-Small), providing insights into how these models process visual and audio inputs without explicit encoders.
papers.title: Encoder-Free Multimodal LLMs Learn Implicit Encoders
papers.tldr: Encoder-free multimodal LLMs appear to develop early Transformer layers that function as implicit, largely modality-independent audio and vision encoders.

papers.abstract: Solving algorithmic tasks with many sequential steps typically requires scaling up transformer depth or chain-of-thought length, incurring unfavorable parameter and inference-compute costs, respectively. Looped transformers, which reuse one block of layers across many iterations, are poised to address this, since they scale effective depth without adding parameters or tokens. Yet, it remains unclear what each iteration is actually computing, or whether the loop merely simulates a deeper untied stack. Here, we study directed permutation traversal, in which a model follows $H$ hops from a starting node and reports the node it reaches, so every intermediate hop has a known ground truth. We find that a minimum effective depth is necessary to solve the task, beyond which the degree of weight tying becomes the determining factor. For instance, a looped transformer with a four-layer block iterated eight times solves the task in every seed, while an identically-trained untied transformer of the same effective depth never does, succeeding only with a lower learning rate or supervision of its intermediate layers. Probing and intervening on the residual stream, we find that the looped model advances through the intermediate nodes gradually, forming a staircase that adapts to its iteration budget, whereas the untied model, at that lower rate, exposes them only in its final layers. Taken together, our results recast looped transformers as iterative program learners, which allocate their iterations to successive steps of the algorithm and solve tasks that identically-trained untied models of the same effective depth do not. Code is available at https://github.com/magnus-sesodia/insidetheloop.
authors: Magnus Sesodia, Juil Sock, Philip Torr, Christian Schroeder de Witt
bullets: Studies directed permutation traversal, where each hop provides a known intermediate target.
Finds that sufficient effective depth is necessary, but weight tying strongly affects successful learning beyond that threshold.
A four-layer block looped for eight iterations solves the task across all seeds, while an equally deep untied model does not under identical training.
Residual-stream analysis shows looped models progressively represent intermediate nodes in an iteration-adaptive staircase.
Results support viewing looped transformers as iterative program learners rather than merely simulated deep stacks.
papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic study of weight-tied/looped transformer architectures and iterative computation, directly relevant to LLM architecture advances.
papers.title: Inside the Loop: A Mechanistic Study of Weight-Tied Transformers on Depth-Bound Algorithmic Tasks
papers.tldr: Weight-tied looped transformers learn algorithmic steps iteratively, solving depth-bound permutation tasks more reliably than equally deep untied models under the same training setup.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires long-horizon instruction-consistent planning and short-horizon local planning in current geometry. Video-action models (VAMs) offer a promising way to learn predictive representations for navigation. However, existing VAMs jointly predict visual futures and local trajectories in a single process, even though they operate at different paces: future prediction remains stable across multiple updates while local trajectories must react to fresh observations. To bridge this gap, we introduce HAVANA, a dual-system VAM that decouples predictive reasoning from reactive local planning. A slow system produces a compact language-conditioned latent plan from observation history, while a fast system combines the latest plan with the current observation to generate local trajectories. Their asynchronous execution enables rapid adaptation without repeated future prediction, and no future video is generated during inference. Experiments on OmniNavBench demonstrate state-of-the-art navigation performance over prior baselines, while real-world deployments further show robust generalization to unseen environments across different robot embodiments. Our code and checkpoints will be available at https://github.com/Anastasiawd/HAVANA.
authors: Dongzhihan Wang
Yi Du
Chen Wang
Xiuxian Li
Liang Xu
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between stable long-horizon prediction and rapidly changing local navigation needs.
Uses a slow system to create a compact, language-conditioned latent plan from observation history.
Uses a fast system to combine the plan with the latest observation and generate local trajectories asynchronously.
Avoids generating future video during inference while enabling rapid adaptation to new observations.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on OmniNavBench and generalizes to unseen real-world environments across robot embodiments.
papers.selection_reason: Presents HAVANA, a dual-system Video-Action Model for Vision-Language Navigation that decouples predictive reasoning from reactive local planning, improving navigation performance.
papers.title: HAVANA: A Hierarchical Video-Action Model for Vision-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: HAVANA improves vision-language navigation by separating slow predictive planning from fast reactive trajectory generation.

papers.abstract: Digital terrain maps (DTMs) are used for landing site selection, terrain-relative navigation, and geological analysis in planetary exploration. Existing state-of-practice reconstruction techniques for creating DTMs from satellite imagery use multi-view stereo, requiring complex pipelines for dealing with camera error, changing illumination, and images with limited disparity. This work introduces Orbital Terrain Networks (OrTeN), a DTM construction method that uses neural inverse rendering to jointly optimize a textured height map and orbital camera corrections from line-scan satellite images. OrTeN operates directly on calibrated line-scan images with pixel values expressed as radiance factor (I/F) and corrects both broad trajectory pose inconsistencies and high-frequency pointing jitter jointly with surface reconstruction during training. Surface-projected patch normalized cross-correlation (NCC) enforces consistency between observations of the same terrain, refining an initial rough reconstruction. A semi-empirical reflectance model and shadow rendering are used to fit surface appearance from multi-date imagery with differing solar illumination. OrTeN requires only calibrated line-scan images and initial camera poses and does not use any structural priors including ranging/depth measurements or initial rough DTMs. OrTeN is evaluated on four planetary imagery datasets. Aligned terrain RMSEs are 2.35 m at Jezero Crater, 2.82 m at Gale Crater, 16.18 m at Olympus Mons, and 0.43 m at McGetchin Crater.
authors: Josef Biberstein, Sertac Karaman
bullets: Targets DTM generation from satellite imagery affected by camera errors, changing illumination, and limited image disparity.
Optimizes a textured height map together with broad trajectory corrections and high-frequency pointing jitter.
Uses surface-projected patch NCC, a reflectance model, and shadow rendering to enforce cross-image consistency across illumination conditions.
Requires calibrated line-scan images and initial camera poses, but no ranging/depth data or structural terrain priors.
Evaluated on four planetary datasets, with aligned terrain RMSEs ranging from 0.43 m to 16.18 m.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces OrTeN, a neural inverse graphics method for joint terrain and camera trajectory reconstruction, which is directly applicable to robot navigation in planetary exploration.
papers.title: OrTeN: Neural Inverse Graphics for Joint Terrain and Line-scan Camera Trajectory Reconstruction
papers.tldr: OrTeN jointly reconstructs planetary terrain and corrects line-scan satellite camera trajectories using neural inverse rendering, without depth measurements or an initial terrain model.

papers.abstract: This paper studies dynamic model routing under uncertainty in multimodal settings, where a system must select and potentially compose multiple models to answer a query. Standard reinforcement learning approaches for routing often suffer from premature convergence to suboptimal models due to noisy rewards and insufficient exploration. We propose a unified vision-language framework (VL-Scout) for efficient multimodal and multi-step reasoning with turn-based reinforcement fusion. First, VL-Scout combines Bayesian priors, policy gradient optimization, and sequential decision-making to enable structured exploration and adaptive inference. A context-dependent Dirichlet belief model allows for epistemic uncertainty over model quality and is updated online based on observed rewards and context-specific evidence, enabling Thompson-style exploration while serving as a prior for regularization. Second, a routing policy is trained via a KL-regularized REINFORCE objective by maximizing a reward-weighted evidence lower bound, where the policy acts as an amortized posterior, and the Dirichlet belief serves as a prior. Third, we introduce a fusion policy trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) or Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), which operates over intermediate model rationales and selects between two actions: CONTINUE or ANSWER, terminating with a generated output. We evaluate VL-Scout on four representative multi-modal benchmarks (MMMU, MMMU-Pro, OKVQA, and RealWorldQA), compared against 11 representative routing and policy optimization baselines. Our method provides consistent performance improvements while reducing premature policy collapse. These results highlight the importance of integrating uncertainty-aware priors with both amortized policy learning and sequential fusion for robust and efficient model selection in discrete action spaces
authors: Selim Furkan Tekin, Ling Liu
bullets: Targets dynamic selection and composition of models for uncertain multimodal queries.
Uses context-dependent Dirichlet beliefs, Bayesian/Thompson-style exploration, and KL-regularized REINFORCE for adaptive routing.
Adds a fusion policy trained with GRPO or RLVR to decide whether to CONTINUE reasoning or ANSWER.
Evaluated on MMMU, MMMU-Pro, OKVQA, and RealWorldQA against 11 baselines.
Reports consistent performance improvements and reduced premature policy collapse, without specifying numeric gains.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a vision-language routing and fusion framework for multimodal reasoning, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Alliance of Stochastic Routing and Reinforcement Fusion for Multi-Model Reasoning
papers.tldr: VL-Scout combines uncertainty-aware routing with reinforcement-based multi-model fusion to improve robust multimodal reasoning and reduce premature policy collapse.

papers.abstract: RL agents trained on a single trajectory-level return face a credit-assignment problem: when a reward arrives many steps after the decision that caused it, every action gets the same signal regardless of causal responsibility. This paper studies Visual Causal-chain Bookmarking (VCBM), which concentrates credit on the decision points that determine an episode's return, via two instantiations. The first targets a fully observed, low-dimensional MDP (a delayed-reward watch-repair task), where VCBM statistically discovers which state components the agent causally controls and estimates per-decision-point action values directly, evaluated against ground truth and RUDDER, an LSTM-based baseline. VCBM converges to 95.07% correct decisions in a mean of 1,532.3 episodes across 20 seeds, versus RUDDER's slower, more variable convergence (mean 3,327.1 episodes; p<0.001); VCBM's discovered causal structure exactly matches ground truth in all seeds. The second targets a partially observed, language-based setting: an LLM agent trained with Leave-One-Out PPO (LOOP) in AppWorld, where causal discovery is intractable and a structural heuristic (state-mutating tool calls) substitutes for it, with credit distributed via retrieval over episodic memory and blended with LOOP's advantage. Over 200 iterations on identical Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct/LoRA/FSDP2 configurations, VCBM-blended LOOP improves task success over plain LOOP (0.354 vs. 0.458), reduces final-step max importance weight, and improves token efficiency, with a small KL exception favouring LOOP. The watch-repair result supports the claim that weighting causally relevant steps is more sample-efficient than an undifferentiated baseline or a learned return-redistribution network; the AppWorld result, limited to one seed per arm by a 2-GPU budget, is a compute-limited demonstration at a harder, natural-language scale, not a statistical confirmation.
authors: Prathap Selvakumar
bullets: Addresses the problem of assigning equal credit to all actions when rewards arrive long after their causes.
In a fully observed watch-repair MDP, VCBM discovers causal state components and directly estimates per-decision action values.
VCBM reached 95.07% correct decisions in a mean of 1,532.3 episodes across 20 seeds, versus 3,327.1 for RUDDER; its causal structure matched ground truth in every seed.
In AppWorld, a retrieval-based heuristic blended with LOOP improved task success from 0.354 to 0.458, while also improving token efficiency and reducing final-step maximum importance weight.
The AppWorld result used one seed per arm and is therefore a compute-limited demonstration rather than statistical confirmation; a small KL metric favored plain LOOP.
papers.selection_reason: Uses retrieval over episodic memory for an LLM agent, relevant to LLM memory mechanisms even though the core focus is credit assignment.
papers.title: Visual Causal-chain Bookmarking: Retrieval-Weighted Credit Assignment for Reinforcement Learning from Delayed Reward
papers.tldr: VCBM improves delayed-reward credit assignment by focusing learning on causally relevant decisions, outperforming undifferentiated or learned return-redistribution baselines in two settings.

papers.abstract: Internal signatures could support monitoring, adaptive computation, and mechanistic analysis, but benchmark prompts can be separable without any shared computational distinction. We test whether a prespecified knowledge/reasoning label defines a reusable internal signature in five contemporary 7B to 31B models. We treat the \textbf{task} as the unit of inference probes hold out complete tasks, labels are permuted across tasks, and the best layer and stream are reselected for every permutation. Raw probes recover an eight-versus-eight-subject MMLU partition in all five models (macro-F1 $0.78$--$0.81$), but prompt text predicts it nearly as well: under an identical probe configuration, the activation advantage is only $0.017$--$0.070$ macro-F1 and is not significant. At the prespecified $0.01$ level, lexical adjustment removes significance while the adjusted states still identify individual subjects, and the selected site changes across task panels and selection rules. Additionally, two released base-training trajectories show no common direction. These pooled layerwise measures recover the task label but identify no transferable knowledge/reasoning signature at the tested sensitivity, which cannot exclude moderate effects. The resulting protocol gives future internal monitors and intervention studies a sequence of tests to pass. Project page: \url{https://parsa-ra.github.io/lmbehave/}.
authors: Parsa Rahimi, Azim Dehghani Amirabad
bullets: Task-held-out probes recover the benchmark partition with macro-F1 0.78–0.81, but prompt text predicts it nearly as well.
Activation-based gains are small (0.017–0.070 macro-F1) and become nonsignificant after lexical adjustment at the prespecified 0.01 level.
The best layer and activation stream vary across task panels and selection rules, indicating poor stability.
Two base-training trajectories show no common direction, further weakening evidence for a shared signature.
The results do not rule out moderate effects, but define tests future monitoring and intervention studies should pass.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates internal representation signatures in modern LLMs, fitting LLM architecture and interpretability interests.
papers.title: Do Knowledge and Reasoning Oriented Benchmarks Induce Stable Representation Signatures in LLMs?
papers.tldr: Across five LLMs, knowledge-versus-reasoning benchmark labels are recoverable but do not produce a stable, transferable internal representation signature under the tested protocol.

papers.abstract: Standard self-attention compares tokens by similarity but does not account for how much of a past state survives to the present. We introduce Dynamical Kernel Attention (DKA), which derives attention from robust estimation of a latent state evolving under stochastic dynamics. As a past state decays toward equilibrium under the dynamics, the information it carries about the present vanishes, bounding the total evidence a head can draw. Unlike recency biases, DKA can abstain when relevant evidence is weak and guarantees a bounded error when old tokens are discarded. DKA preserves the parallel structure and computational cost of standard attention. We present the model and its theory; empirical evaluation is deferred to a subsequent version.
authors: Peter Racioppo
bullets: Standard self-attention measures similarity but ignores how much information from past states remains relevant to the present.
DKA derives attention by robustly estimating a latent state evolving under stochastic dynamics.
Information from past states decays toward equilibrium, limiting the total evidence an attention head can use.
Unlike simple recency biases, DKA can abstain when relevant evidence is weak and provides error guarantees when old tokens are discarded.
The abstract presents theory and the model; empirical evaluation is deferred to future work.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes an attention mechanism with bounded-error token discarding, directly relevant to efficient attention and token eviction.
papers.title: Dynamical Kernel Attention: Estimating the Present from a Record of the Past
papers.tldr: Dynamical Kernel Attention incorporates stochastic state dynamics into attention, enabling principled decay, abstention under weak evidence, and bounded error from discarding old tokens without added computational cost.

papers.abstract: Long-term personalized agents are required to reason over distributed history across modalities and evolving dialogue states. While existing flat cross-modal methods compress visual evidence prematurely and struggle with temporally stale observations, they neglect the necessity to unify multimodal and cross-session evidence. Crucially, raw multimodal memories are inherently entangled and heterogeneous, making fine-grained visual grounding and cross-modal reasoning computationally prohibitive. To this end, we present latent multimodal memory reasoning, i.e., LMMR, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that shifts long-term multimodal memory organization into a continuous latent space. Specifically, (i) instead of converting images to text and relying on static retrieval, LMMR maps both textual hidden states and visual patch features into a shared Sparse Autoencoder concept space, establishing sparse activations as common semantic addresses to dynamically construct a turn-level multimodal memory graph. (ii) A graph encoder then aggregates cross-modal and temporal dependencies across the task-specific latent subgraph, injecting the graph readout as a continuous residual rollout into the generation backbone while retaining native visual tokens to preserve fine-grained details. Extensive experiments on nine Mem-Gallery tasks and twelve MemEye settings demonstrate that LMMR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in capturing complex multimodal dependencies while enabling faithful and grounded responses.
authors: Cai Ke, Xinghao Chen, Yuanchen Bei, Yuni Lai, Keyu Chen, Ruizhi Qiao, Siyu An, Junnan Dong, Ruifeng Xu, Xing Sun
bullets: Addresses distributed, evolving multimodal history, including temporally stale observations and heterogeneous raw memories.
Maps text hidden states and visual patch features into a shared Sparse Autoencoder concept space with sparse semantic addresses.
Builds turn-level multimodal memory graphs and uses a graph encoder to aggregate cross-modal and temporal dependencies.
Injects graph representations into the generation backbone while retaining native visual tokens for fine-grained grounding.
Experiments across nine Mem-Gallery tasks and twelve MemEye settings report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in multimodal dependency capture and response faithfulness.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a neuro-symbolic framework for long-term multimodal memory reasoning, mapping visual and textual evidence into a shared latent space to handle spatiotemporal dependencies.
papers.title: Latent Multimodal Memory Reasoning
papers.tldr: LMMR organizes long-term multimodal memories in a shared latent concept space and reasons over their temporal and cross-modal relationships for more faithful responses.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning on agent trajectories is an effective way to improve coding agents, but selecting useful training examples requires more than identifying successful runs. A resolved patch may follow inefficient reasoning or unnecessary tool use, while a failed run may still contain useful intermediate steps. Training pipelines therefore rely on rules and qualitative assessments to filter trajectories, yet designing these filters typically requires substantial human expertise, and validating improvements through repeated training and evaluation is expensive. We introduce MetaCurate, a training-free framework that evolves executable trajectory curation filters using pairwise LLM judgments. Disagreements between the filter's rankings and the judge's preferences provide targeted feedback for jointly revising its rules, rubric, and aggregation policy. The resulting filter scores trajectories independently, so pairwise comparisons are required only during search. Starting from a blank filter, MetaCurate autonomously discovers a curation strategy that achieves competitive downstream performance without task-specific handwritten criteria. We validate downstream utility through controlled SFT experiments on our uncurated trajectory pool and the Nemotron v3 SWE dataset, with random selection and hand-authored filtering as baselines. In our experiments, MetaCurate achieves the highest mean SWE-Verified score among the compared methods, including hand-authored rule-based filtering and a training-loop baseline whose search costs 3.5x as much.
authors: Donghoon Kim
Seunghyuk Oh
Kevin Galim
Minseo Kim
Minjae Lee
Younghyun Kim
Wooseok Seo
Hyung Il Koo
Wonjun Kang
bullets: Successful trajectories may contain inefficient reasoning, while failed runs can include useful intermediate steps, making curation difficult.
The framework uses pairwise LLM judgments to identify ranking disagreements and revise a filter’s rules, rubric, and aggregation policy.
After search, the learned filter scores trajectories independently, avoiding pairwise comparisons during deployment.
Controlled SFT experiments on an uncurated pool and the Nemotron v3 SWE dataset found the highest mean SWE-Verified score among compared methods, including hand-authored filtering.
The approach is training-free during curation search and reportedly costs less than a training-loop baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a training-free framework (MetaCurate) for evolving curation filters of agent data using LLM judgments, addressing the management and quality of training data (memory) for LLM agents.
papers.title: MetaCurate: Evolving Curation Filters for High-Quality Agentic Coding Data
papers.tldr: MetaCurate automatically evolves executable filters to select high-value coding-agent trajectories without hand-written task-specific rules or repeated training during filter search.

papers.abstract: Consumer phones and wearables increasingly collect physiological time-series data, yet most mobile systems treat these streams as summaries or text rather than as temporal evidence. This representation is poorly matched to personal health systems that need to retrieve, route, or summarize sensor evidence while preserving temporal structure. Cloud-hosted time-series language models avoid smartphone limits, but they repeatedly move sensitive physiology off the device and add latency and per-query compute cost. Mobile model alternatives that aggregate time-series data into statistical features or serialize raw samples as text either compress temporal structure or exhaust the context and memory budgets of small on-device models. We present PocketTSLM, a mobile-native deployment of OpenTSLM SoftPrompt, the soft-prompt variant of the OpenTSLM time-series language model. PocketTSLM runs fully on a consumer smartphone by injecting encoded time-series windows as embeddings instead of tokenizing time series as text. A numerical parity protocol verifies identical greedy-decoded token sequences between the Swift port and a Python reference using Apple's MLX machine-learning framework. Answers also match the PyTorch reference, although rationale wording can differ. An on-device context-economics benchmark compares the soft-prompt path with a text-serialized baseline on the same backbone. In our benchmark format, soft-prompting uses approximately 12 times fewer time-series tokens and reduces prompt-prefill cost. PocketTSLM processes 30-second Sleep-EDF electroencephalography clips for sleep staging and a 1,000-sample (10 s) 12-lead electrocardiogram clip from ECG-QA. In comparison, text-serialized baselines exceed the phone's context or memory budget at longer time-series windows. All inference runs entirely on the device, with no health data transmitted during inference.
authors: Max Rosenblattl
Nikhil Krishnaswamy
Leon Nissen
Manuel Milling
Nicolas Zumarraga
Ning Wang
Thomas Kaar
Robert Jakob
Björn W. Schuller
Elgar Fleisch
Patrick Langer
Paul Schmiedmayer
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between text-based mobile models and temporally structured physiological data, while avoiding cloud privacy, latency, and compute costs.
Injects encoded time-series windows as embeddings rather than serializing samples as text, preserving temporal input within mobile context limits.
Implements the OpenTSLM SoftPrompt model in Swift using Apple’s MLX framework and verifies numerical parity with a Python reference.
Processes Sleep-EDF EEG clips for sleep staging and 1,000-sample, 12-lead ECG clips from ECG-QA on a consumer smartphone.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a soft-prompting approach for on-device time-series language models that significantly reduces the number of tokens required compared to text serialization, improving memory and context efficiency.
papers.title: PocketTSLM: Deploying an On-Device Soft-Prompt Time-Series Language Model for Privacy-Preserving Smartphone Reasoning
papers.tldr: PocketTSLM brings soft-prompt time-series language modeling to smartphones, enabling private on-device reasoning over physiological signals without transmitting health data.

papers.abstract: Latent reasoning replaces natural-language chains of thought with compact continuous "soft-token" representations, reducing the number of intermediate tokens that must be decoded autoregressively. We use a small external encoder to induce latent reasoning in a frozen backbone model. The encoder iteratively maps the backbone's hidden states to new latent blocks, constructing a latent reasoning prefix, after which the frozen model writes its remaining reasoning and its answer as text. Our method, INTACT, trains this encoder through distillation to reproduce the effect of written reasoning steps while keeping the model's behavior close to that of the frozen backbone, and then reinforces it on answer correctness. Across four frozen backbones from 1B to 8B, INTACT improves both GSM8K and average out-of-domain accuracy, including GSM8K gains from 75.8% to 79.3% on Llama-3.2-3B and from 77.6% to 79.7% on Qwen2.5-3B. It also reduces end-to-end latency per problem by 19% on Llama-3.2-3B and outperforms the evaluated latent-reasoning baselines at the 3B and 8B scales. Beyond the mathematics setting, the same recipe trained on a multi-domain corpus improves the frozen backbone on twelve evaluation benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, and commonsense, without task-specific adaptation.
authors: Kutay Tire
Atula Tejaswi
Haris Vikalo
Sujay Sanghavi
bullets: Uses a small external encoder to iteratively transform frozen-backbone hidden states into a latent reasoning prefix.
Trains the encoder by distilling written reasoning, preserving the backbone’s behavior, then reinforces it using answer correctness.
Across four frozen backbones from 1B–8B parameters, it improves GSM8K and average out-of-domain accuracy.
On Llama-3.2-3B, GSM8K rises from 75.8% to 79.3% and latency falls by 19%.
A multi-domain version improves performance across twelve mathematics, science, and commonsense benchmarks without task-specific adaptation.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a method (INTACT) to induce latent reasoning in frozen LLM backbones to reduce latency, directly addressing LLM efficiency and reasoning architectures.
papers.title: INTACT: Inducing Latent Reasoning on a Frozen Backbone
papers.tldr: INTACT adds compact latent reasoning to frozen language models, improving accuracy while reducing inference latency.

papers.abstract: While LLM-based agent systems have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in reasoning and solving complex real-world tasks, they also come with substantial token consumption and inference latency, limiting their practical deployment. To enhance the efficiency of agent systems, recent efforts have focused on transferring agentic capabilities from large-scale models to small language models (SLMs) via supervised fine-tuning-based distillation. Nevertheless, as interaction trajectories grow longer, involving extended reasoning-action chains and extensive environmental feedback, distilled student agents tend to experience progress stagnation: becoming trapped in unproductive loops characterized by persistent failed strategies and difficulty making meaningful progress. Our systematic analysis shows that this phenomenon consistently occurs across diverse SLMs and task domains. To address this issue, we propose Progress-Aware Distillation (ProD), which explicitly detects and penalizes stagnation in student-generated trajectories. ProD encodes the stagnation gap between student and teacher into an adaptive margin for dynamically penalizing possible stagnation. By iteratively applying this procedure, ProD enables student agents to progressively approximate teacher behavior. Extensive experiments involving 8 SLMs, ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters, on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrate that ProD substantially mitigates progress stagnation while enhancing both the success rates and task-completion efficiency of distilled SLM agents.
authors: Yuanpu Cao
Saket Sathe
Hanyu Wang
Ziyi Yin
Fenglong Ma
Jinghui Chen
bullets: Distilled SLM agents can become trapped in unproductive loops during long reasoning-action trajectories.
The stagnation problem appears consistently across diverse SLMs and task domains.
ProD detects stagnation and converts the student–teacher stagnation gap into an adaptive penalty margin.
Iterative progress-aware distillation helps students increasingly approximate teacher behavior.
Experiments across 8 SLMs (0.6B–8B) and in- and out-of-domain benchmarks show improved success rates and efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses a critical issue in LLM agents (stagnation) and proposes a novel distillation technique (Progress-Aware Distillation) to improve SLM agent performance.
papers.title: Progress-Aware Distillation for Mitigating Stagnation in Small Language Model Agents
papers.tldr: Progress-Aware Distillation reduces stagnation in distilled small language model agents, improving task success and completion efficiency across models and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Flow policies capture rich and diverse action distributions, and fine-tuning them with off-policy RL to improve beyond the demonstrations has drawn growing interest. However, fine-tuning a flow policy against a learned value function is not trivial, because the policy generates its action over many flow steps. Adjoint matching offers a principled way to update the flow model itself by propagating value information from the final action back to each flow step, but it requires a vector--Jacobian product through the policy at every step, a cost that grows with the number of flow steps and the policy size. We observe that the batch-averaged velocity Jacobian of pretrained flow policies concentrates on its diagonal. Motivated by this finding, we derive a closed-form scalar adjoint that scales the value gradient at the final action by the flow time, eliminating the per-step vector--Jacobian products. We further find that controlling the critic's value at policy-generated actions is particularly important under the scalar adjoint. Based on these findings, we propose Q-learning with Scalar Adjoint Matching (SQAM), which combines the scalar adjoint with a value penalty at those actions. SQAM's gains concentrate on the four hardest OGBench domains, where its success rate exceeds that of the strongest baseline in each domain by 18 to 35 percentage points. To test whether SQAM extends to large pretrained policies, we also fine-tune a vision-language-action policy on a real bimanual robot. SQAM improves over supervised fine-tuning on all three tasks.
authors: Yonghoon Dong
Minsung Yoon
Jaehyuk Kim
Jungwoo Park
Changyeon Kim
Jinwoo Shin
bullets: Flow policies require value information to be propagated through many generation steps, making standard adjoint matching expensive.
The method uses a scalar adjoint that scales the final-action value gradient by flow time, avoiding per-step vector–Jacobian products.
SQAM adds a value penalty on policy-generated actions to control critic estimates.
On the four hardest OGBench domains, SQAM exceeds the strongest baseline by 18–35 percentage points in success rate.
It also improves over supervised fine-tuning across all three tasks in a real bimanual-robot evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: RL fine-tuning of flow policies and VLA policies for robot control; fits Embodied AI.
papers.title: Q-Learning with Scalar Adjoint Matching
papers.tldr: SQAM makes off-policy RL fine-tuning of flow policies cheaper by replacing costly per-step adjoint computations with a scalar approximation and stabilizing critic values at generated actions.

papers.abstract: Humans perceive far more in a scene than what is explicitly depicted: a single glance captures past causes and future trajectories; a quick peek determines if a vehicle can fit between two parked cars; a few seconds of video reveals who holds authority in a room; and a fleeting clip highlights subtle abstract patterns like unwritten rules or hidden labels. This capacity reflects a form of humanity's sixth sense: an intuitive reasoning mechanism that recovers implicit information beyond raw sensory perception. Crucially, this rapid, zero-shot visual intuition underpins everyday navigation and social interaction, making it a vital capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) deployed alongside people. Existing visual benchmarks, however, target either deliberate expert-level analysis in academic and mathematical domains or low-level perception, leaving the intuitive reasoning that people perform largely untested. To bridge this gap, we introduce Humanity's Sixth Sense (HSS), a benchmark for intuitive visual reasoning. HSS spans diverse image and video inputs, organizes items under a structured taxonomy, and pairs each with human-written prompts probing the implicit temporal, spatial, social, and abstract structure that people infer at a glance. Frontier MLLMs fall short of human performance: participants reach 93.1% accuracy, while the strongest model, GPT-6-astra, reaches only 53.6% even at maximum reasoning effort. Despite excelling in many complex tasks that require advanced perception and knowledge, current models still struggle significantly on these visual tasks that are intuitive for humans. We further explore agentic setup that apply dynamic visual manipulation to HSS, which narrows but does not close the gap. HSS establishes intuitive visual reasoning as a measurable axis and directs attention to a capability that scaling on current benchmarks has so far left behind.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) adapts frozen large multimodal models (LMMs) to new tasks from a few demonstrations (demos), but re-encodes them at every query, where each demo image adds up to hundreds of visual tokens. Demo-free methods remove this cost with a compact task state. However, they add it at locations searched per task or at every decoder layer, where task parameters grow with depth. Moreover, inserted tokens or keys cannot change how the original prompt divides its attention within a layer. To address these issues, we propose Structured Task Adaptation via Embeddings (STAVE), which replaces demos with two task-specific vectors added to existing input embeddings. Specifically, a readout vector updates the answer-producing tokens and a context vector updates the other structural token groups. Both are trained with answer labels on prompts with and without demos. We justify these design choices theoretically using a first-order analysis of the loss and a margin bound. Extensive experiments on six LMMs and five large language models show that STAVE matches or outperforms state-of-the-art methods on multimodal tasks with far fewer task parameters and surpasses 15-shot ICL and prior task vectors on 18 text tasks, all at zero-shot inference cost.
authors: Xi Ding
Naichen Shi
Jiawei Zhang
bullets: Addresses ICL’s costly repeated demo encoding and the parameter growth of prior demo-free adaptation methods.
Adds a readout vector to answer-producing tokens and a context vector to other structural token groups.
Trains both vectors using answer labels on prompts with and without demonstrations.
Supported by a first-order loss analysis and a margin bound.
Experiments across six LMMs, five LLMs, multimodal tasks, and 18 text tasks show performance matching or exceeding prior methods, including 15-shot ICL, without demo-time inference cost.
papers.selection_reason: Task adaptation via two vectors for LMMs; fits multimodal foundation models and efficient adaptation.
papers.title: Two Vectors Replace In-Context Demos: Structured Task Adaptation via Embeddings
papers.tldr: STAVE replaces in-context demonstrations with two task-specific embedding vectors that enable compact, zero-shot task adaptation for language and multimodal models.

papers.abstract: Scaling robot data and model capacity has improved Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, but further progress is constrained by the high cost of robotic data. Verifier-guided test-time scaling offers an efficient alternative by sampling multiple action candidates and selecting the one most likely to lead to task success at inference time. Existing classification-based verifiers learn from trajectory-level outcomes but treat all visited states equally, even though their value for candidate discrimination can vary across a trajectory. At many states, plausible actions are similar and provide limited discrimination signal, while only a sparse set of decision-critical states admits meaningfully different actions that can substantially affect downstream outcomes. To address this, we propose DiVeR, which estimates decision criticality from the dispersion of sampled action representations. DiVeR then uses this signal to reweight verifier learning toward states where action selection is most consequential, without requiring step-level annotations or additional environment interaction. Across LIBERO, RoboCasa, and real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 robot, DiVeR consistently improves task success through more effective verifier-guided action selection, while adding negligible verifier inference overhead.
authors: Seongheon Park
Heecheol Kim
Shulin Tian
Lilika Makabe
Namiko Saito
Katsushi Ikeuchi
